title: Updating a post when the answer changes
metaTitle: Update a post when the answer changes
excerpt: When a tool, a threshold, or a law changes, update the post and the date. A stale how-to that still ranks is a way to lose trust.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, a street that keeps moving while the map stays printed.

faqs.question: When should we update a post instead of writing a new one?
faqs.answer: Update the existing post when the question is the same and the answer has changed. A new tool default, a new threshold, or a revised law belongs on the URL people already trust. Write a new post when the decision is different, not when you want a second chance at the same query.

faqs.question: Should we change the date if we fix a typo?
faqs.answer: Change the date when the content substantially changes, and leave it alone for a typo. A fresh date on an unchanged page is a trick, and Google's people-first guidance treats it as one. A changed recommendation should be visible.

faqs.question: What if the old advice is already ranking?
faqs.answer: That is the urgent case, not a reason to leave it. A stale how-to that still ranks is teaching the wrong lesson to the most people. Update it, keep the URL if the question is unchanged, and redirect only if you had to replace the page with a different one.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A content refresh strategy can be this small: when a tool, a threshold, or a law changes, update the post and the date. A stale how-to that still ranks is a way to lose trust, because the people most ready to believe you are the ones who find the old answer first.

New posts do not fix old ones. The old URL keeps teaching.

## Update the page people already use

If the question is stable, keep the URL. Founders bookmark how-tos. Other pages link to them. A search result points at them. Replacing a changed answer with a brand-new slug, and leaving the old slug alive, splits the trust you have already earned. Update the body. Say what changed, in a sentence, if a returning reader would otherwise think they had imagined the old advice.

This is ordinary maintenance, like fixing a link or a price on a project page. It is not a campaign. The studios that fall behind are the ones that treat every correction as a new content idea, because new ideas feel like progress and edits feel like chores. The edit is the progress. The new idea can wait until there is a new question.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the content has easily verified factual errors, and it warns against changing the date to seem fresh when the content has not substantially changed. Those two lines should govern the habit. Real change, visible date. No real change, no new date. It also warns against adding or removing piles of pages mainly to make a site look fresh. A refresh program that exists to "keep the blog active" will manufacture edits. A refresh program that exists because a recommendation would now be wrong will not.

Read the page as if you were about to follow it on a client project. If you would not follow it, it is late.

## What counts as a change

A tool changes when the steps change. A Next.js metadata field moves. A Vercel setting is renamed. A Figma export behaves differently. The screenshot and the sentence that names the menu are now lying. Fix both. A threshold changes when a number you cited is no longer the number the vendor or the standard uses. Do not keep a figure because the paragraph was elegant. A law or a platform rule changes when the thing you told people was allowed, required, or safe has shifted. Accessibility requirements, privacy defaults, and checkout rules belong in this pile. When you are unsure, check the primary document, then change the sentence or remove it.

What does not count: a new synonym you wish you had targeted, a desire for a longer page, a seasonal urge to look busy. Those are rewrites in search of a motive. They waste the URL. They also create diff noise, so a later, necessary update is harder to see.

Public work can date a post without any tool changing. If you described a way of building that Hanabi no longer uses, correct it. If you described Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, or another public project inaccurately, correct it. Do not "refresh" a case study by inflating it. Accuracy is the whole of the update.

Keep a short log at the bottom or in the CMS: date, and one line on what changed. "March: canonical advice updated after the host redirect changed." A log beats a mystery. It also stops you from bumping the date for a comma fix, because the line would embarrass you.

## A stale how-to still in the results

The dangerous page is not the forgotten one. It is the one that still ranks. It has the links, the history, and the confident tone. A founder follows it on a Thursday and breaks a launch. They will not blame the year the world changed. They will blame the studio that sounded sure.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) describes a related failure. When a page is reused and the title element still carries an old year, while the visible heading has moved on, Google may replace the title. Obsolete titles are a known problem. Obsolete steps are worse, and Google will not quietly rewrite your tutorial into the current truth. That repair is yours. If the title says "2022" and the steps are for a later interface, you do not have a title problem. You have a page that teaches the wrong clicks.

When you fix it, fix the promise in the title and the excerpt too. A title that claims a checklist for a platform version you no longer mention is the same class of bug as a wrong step. The share image, if it states a year or a figure, has to change with the page. Otherwise the card keeps arguing with the article in every chat where the link gets pasted.

If you cannot stand behind the updated answer, unpublish the page or replace the steps with a clear "this changed, here is what we recommend now," even if the new recommendation is shorter. A short true page outranks a long false one in the only ranking that matters, which is whether a reader was helped.

## Edit, or write the successor

Edit when the spine is right. The question, the audience, and the order of the decisions still hold. You are replacing facts, examples, and a paragraph of advice.

Write a successor when the decision itself changed. "How we used to set up previews" and "how previews should work now" might be one page if the old way is only a caution. They are two pages if both audiences still exist and would be misled by a merge. If you write the successor, redirect the old URL when the old URL would mislead, or keep the old URL and point it at the new one with a note. Do not let both rank as if both were current.

A successor is not an excuse to keep the stale page for the traffic. The traffic is people. Send them to the current answer.

On a Hanabi site the practical home for this is the same markdown or CMS field as the original piece, plus the metadata around it. You should not need a developer to correct a paragraph. You do need a developer, or a careful editor, when the correction is a route, a redirect, or a feed entry. Decide which kind of change it is before you start, so a wording fix does not become a surprise deploy, and a route change does not get done halfway in the CMS.

## Redirects and the sentences around the page

Internal links rot in a specific way. They quote the old advice in the anchor. "Use the 2021 limit" as the link text, pointing at a page that now explains a different limit, is a bug even after the target is fixed. Search the site for the old figure, the old menu name, and the old recommendation. Update the sentences that send people in. A hub that summarizes the spoke in a clause can become the new source of the stale claim, because you fixed the long page and forgot the map.

The feed needs a decision. A substantial correction can be an updated item, with a summary that says what changed. A silent date bump on an item people already read feels like a reprint. If your reader marks items read, an update may not show at all unless you treat it as new. For a changed recommendation, treat it as new. For a typo, do not.

Canonicals should stay put if the URL stays put. Do not invent a "refreshed" duplicate at a new path and canonicalize the old one. You have created the split you spend other essays preventing. One address. New words.

## A cadence for maintenance

Maintenance needs a slot, or it will lose to new work every week. Once a month, open the ten pages that bring the most serious visits or the most conversations. Skim for tool names, numbers, and steps. You are not rewriting. You are hunting for claims that would embarrass you on a call this afternoon.

Keep a list of dependencies: which posts mention a product's UI, which mention a metric from a cited source, which mention a law. When you hear that one of those changed, you know the short list to open. This is the unglamorous version of a content program, and it is the one that keeps a careful studio from becoming a confident one that is wrong.

Do not refresh by adding a section of generic advice to make the page longer. Length was never the defect. A wrong step beside three new paragraphs of scene-setting is still a wrong step. Cut the scene-setting if you need room. Keep the correction near the place a reader will act.

If you cite an outside document, re-read it before you re-cite it. Standards move. A paraphrase that was fair last year can become a slant. The approved sources you rely on, whether that is a Google documentation page or a WCAG overview, should be opened, not remembered. Memory is how stale pages congratulate themselves.

## Trust after the update

A good update is visible and modest. "Updated in September: the host redirect is now the bare domain, and the steps below follow that." No apology tour. No pretend that you always said this. The reader can handle a change of mind better than a silent one. Future you can handle it better too, when you are trying to remember why the screenshot looks different from the one in an old proposal.

Then leave the page alone until the next real change. A page that is edited every week for tone will never feel stable enough to trust, including by the person who maintains it. Stability between real changes is part of the promise.

When the words are current, the links that point at them still have to sound like a person. [Internal links that sound like a person](/blog/internal-links-that-sound-like-a-person) is the next piece, because an updated page with a trail of "read more" around it wastes the correction.

If a whole set of pages has drifted and you want a second pair of eyes on what still matches the offer, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the three URLs you are least sure you would follow yourself.
